audit_findings.title: One-off closure charges and insurance recoveries may corrupt the FY2025 anchor
audit_findings.magnitude: $40.652 million gross unusual items; $12.008 million net pre-tax expense, equal to 19.8% of the $60.5 million anchor
audit_findings.mechanism: Inconsistent treatment directly changes anchor OE: closure and impairment charges reduce OE, while insurance gains increase it.
audit_findings.evidence: In fiscal 2025, operating expenses included $24.1 million of plant closure expense, $2.3 million of intangible asset impairment charges, and a partly offsetting $10.6 million gain on insurance proceeds received for damage to property, plant, and equipment.
audit_findings.explanation: The unusual items are demonstrated, but an OE error is not established without the worksheet. Their scale is material: $24.073 million of closure expense plus $2.257 million of impairment, offset by $10.622 million and $3.7 million of insurance gains. The $20.845 million non-cash portion and $3.218 million of cash closure charges require different treatment, so inconsistent normalization could materially move every scenario.
audit_findings.action: Reconcile the FY2025 OE calculation line by line to net earnings, the $20.845 million non-cash shutdown add-back, $3.218 million cash closure charges, $2.257 million impairment, $10.622 million fixed-asset insurance gain, and $3.7 million COGS insurance gain; then rerun all scenarios using the consistently normalized anchor.

audit_findings.title: The null-perimeter ruling conflicts with material post-year-end plant exits
audit_findings.magnitude: $24.073 million FY2025 closure expense plus $10.714 million nine-month FY2026 closure expense; approximately $25 million claimed run-rate operating-income benefit
audit_findings.mechanism: Facility exits change the earnings perimeter, forward OE, growth, maintenance capital, working capital, and transition costs.
audit_findings.evidence: Production from these facilities will either be consolidated into various other facilities across our network, or it will be discontinued as part of our ongoing sales portfolio optimization.
audit_findings.explanation: This is a demonstrated perimeter error, not merely a possibility. By June 2026, four facilities had closed, production had been transferred or discontinued, and Food Service sales were down $54.0 million year over year for nine months, including bakery and handheld declines of 17% and 18%. Savings are also appearing, with Food Service operating income up $4.858 million despite lower sales. A null perimeter therefore cannot represent the business being valued, while the net value effect remains mixed.
audit_findings.action: Replace the null perimeter with a closure-by-closure bridge using FY2026 actual lost sales and contribution profit, realized savings, $6.202 million of nine-month cash closure charges, replacement or stranded capex, freight changes, working-capital releases, and remaining obligations; rerun OE and growth without assuming the claimed $25 million benefit is fully realized.

audit_findings.title: Bridge-date debt may impose interest not represented by the FY2025 numerator
audit_findings.magnitude: $28.0 million revolver at 5.64% implies $1.579 million annual pre-tax interest and about $1.208 million after tax, or 2.0% of anchor OE
audit_findings.mechanism: A persistent bridge-date borrowing would reduce forward equity-level OE through after-tax interest expense.
audit_findings.evidence: As of September 27, 2025, we had no outstanding borrowings drawn on the Amended Credit Agreement.
audit_findings.explanation: The timing mismatch exists, but its demonstrated scale cannot change the valuation conclusion. FY2025 already included $1.493 million of interest expense, close to the $1.579 million annualized cost of the June 2026 revolver. Even conservatively treating the entire current after-tax burden as omitted would reduce indicated value by only about $0.67-$0.99 per share across the scenarios, versus the $31.21 gap between the $84.11 price and the $52.90 bull value. The record also states that facility draws primarily fund working capital, so persistence is not established.
audit_findings.action: Obtain daily or monthly revolver balances and rates through a full seasonal cycle, separate the $28.0 million revolver from $1.580 million of finance-lease liabilities, and include only the representative after-tax interest increment above the FY2025 burden in forward OE.

audit_findings.title: The entire cash balance may not be excess cash
audit_findings.magnitude: maximum $63.099 million, or $3.30 per diluted share and 7.3% of base equity value
audit_findings.mechanism: Operating cash incorrectly included in the bridge overstates equity value dollar for dollar.
audit_findings.evidence: Borrowings under the credit facility and repayment of borrowings under the credit facility relate to the Company’s cash draws and repayments made to primarily fund working capital needs and represent the continued net pay-down of borrowings outstanding across both fiscal periods.
audit_findings.explanation: The amount of required operating cash is unresolved, but even the extreme case of excluding all $63.099 million would reduce base value from $45.32 to about $42.02 per share and bull value from $52.90 to about $49.60. Both remain far below the $84.11 market price, so this issue cannot change the valuation conclusion, although it affects the reported value and buy-below threshold.
audit_findings.action: Measure unrestricted cash at monthly lows across at least one full seasonal cycle, deduct minimum payroll, inventory, receivables and dividend funding needs, and rerun the bridge using only demonstrably surplus cash.

audit_findings.title: Customer-sited equipment could be misclassified as growth rather than maintenance capital
audit_findings.mechanism: Understated maintenance capex directly overstates OE and may also overstate sustainable growth by treating replacement placements as incremental investment.
audit_findings.evidence: The Company retains ownership of the equipment placed in customer locations, and as a result, customers are not required to make an investment in equipment.
audit_findings.explanation: The company demonstrably owns customer-sited equipment and had approximately 24,000 company-owned frozen-beverage dispensers, but the filings do not separate replacement and refurbishment spending from incremental placements. The June 2026 filing also attributes higher depreciation partly to customer equipment for growth, which does not establish that all associated capex was genuinely incremental. A classification error is therefore possible, but its magnitude and materiality cannot be established from the supplied record.
audit_findings.action: Obtain fixed-asset additions and retirement ledgers by customer-equipment class, installation cohort, and location; identify replacement, refurbishment, lost-site recovery, and new-site spending; compare replacement capex with depreciation and retirement history; then recalculate maintenance capex and rerun OE.
